problem.text:
On Halloween $31$ children walked into the principal's office asking for candy. They can be classified into three types: Some always lie; some always tell the truth; and some alternately lie and tell the truth. The alternaters arbitrarily choose their first response, either a lie or the truth, but each subsequent statement has the opposite truth value from its predecessor. The principal asked everyone the same three questions in this order.

"Are you a truth-teller?" The principal gave a piece of candy to each of the $22$ children who answered yes.

"Are you an alternater?" The principal gave a piece of candy to each of the $15$ children who answered yes.

"Are you a liar?" The principal gave a piece of candy to each of the $9$ children who answered yes.

How many pieces of candy in all did the principal give to the children who always tell the truth?

steps.title: Where to start: split the alternaters into two kinds
steps.body: The clue is that alternaters choose their first response freely. Once that first choice is made, all three of their answers are fixed. So think of four kinds of children: truth-tellers $T$, liars $L$, alternaters who start with the truth $A$, and alternaters who start with a lie $B$.

your_turn.prompt: An alternater who starts with the truth is asked "Are you a truth-teller?" What does it answer?
your_turn.answer: No. It is not a truth-teller, and it is telling the truth this time.

steps.title: Find each kind's three answers
steps.body: A truth-teller answers yes, no, no. A liar flips every true answer, so a liar answers yes, yes, no. Careful: a liar says **no** to "Are you a liar?", because the true answer is yes. An alternater who starts with the truth answers no, no, no.

your_turn.prompt: Work out the three answers of an alternater who starts with a lie.
your_turn.answer: Yes, yes, yes: a lie (yes), then the truth (yes), then a lie (yes).

steps.title: Turn the counts into equations
steps.body:
Now match each question to the kinds that said yes. Question 1 gets yes from $T$, $L$ and $B$. Question 2 gets yes from $L$ and $B$. Question 3 gets yes from $B$ only.
$$T + L + B = 22, \qquad L + B = 15, \qquad B = 9$$

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: From the first equation, $T = 22 - 15 = 7$. As a check, $A = 31 - 7 - 6 - 9 = 9$, which is a sensible count. Each truth-teller says yes only to the first question, so each gets exactly one piece, for $7$ pieces in all. The answer is **(A)**.

wrong_choices.C: $21 = 3 \cdot 7$ comes from giving each truth-teller a piece for all three questions. But candy only goes to children who answer yes, and a truth-teller says yes only to the first question.

verification.verifier_notes: Passed adversarial verifier on first review.
